<reason>Side A wins on the two decisive clashes. First, B's entire alternative route (targeted enforcement via discovery) was exposed as circular: A's Q1 asked how enforcement finds discrimination without visible facts, B answered "a worker who suspects can file," and A closed the loop—suspicion needs a fact, and secrecy hides it. B never repaired this, repeating "discovery opens once someone files" in the closing without addressing how suspicion arises (the Ledbetter point). Second, B's core harm mechanism—that within-band pay or retention bonuses become litigable "confessions"—was undercut by the motion's own scope (bands and aggregate rates, not individual pay), and A showed the tools (headroom, bonuses, equity, off-cycle moves) survive. B's best moments were real: the public-sector category-error rebuttal, the worker-mobility reframe, and "clean number, not higher number" were inventive. But B's gaming logic was partially turned ("you cannot game a promotion metric upward by promoting less"), and its late answers grew more assertive than mechanized. A's weighing—friction for firms with HR departments versus a market failure with no alternative remedy on the table—survived intact. Both sides were disciplined, format-compliant, and rhetorically sharp; A simply left fewer live burdens unanswered.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's exposure of the circularity in B's alternative: Q1 forced B to rest enforcement on "a worker who suspects," and A's closing crystallized that discovery needs a claim, a claim needs suspicion, and suspicion needs exactly the fact secrecy hides—B never answered this, making it the debate's decisive unresolved point.</best_rebuttal>
